items.q: Consent means a person agrees, clearly and freely, to how their data is used.
items.why: Valid consent is informed, specific and freely given.

items.q: Privacy rules such as GDPR only apply to companies based in Europe.
items.why: They apply based on whose data is being used, not only where the company sits.

items.q: A consent box that is already ticked is a good example of valid consent.
items.why: Pre-ticked boxes are not a clear sign of agreement.

items.q: Personal data can include online identifiers such as device IDs and IP addresses.
items.why: Anything that can point to a person, directly or indirectly, can count as personal data.

items.q: Opting out should be as easy as opting in.
items.why: Regulators expect withdrawing consent to be as simple as giving it.

items.q: Hashing an email address always makes it anonymous.
items.why: A hashed email can often still be matched back to the person, so it is usually still personal data.

items.q: The TCF is a framework for passing privacy choices between publishers and ad partners.
items.why: It gives the industry a common way to record and share consent signals.

items.q: Contextual targeting needs data about the individual user.
items.why: It uses the content of the page, not a profile of the person.

items.q: Data minimisation means collecting only the data you actually need.
items.why: Less data collected means less risk and fewer obligations.

items.q: Data about children usually gets extra protection.
items.why: Many rules set stricter conditions for children’s data.
